claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 can be homogenized in a high-temperature BCC phase above approximately 1000°C.
Phase stability in high-temperature BCC Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between the thermodynamic driving force for Al chemical ordering and kinetic limitations on Al diffusion.
Formation of Al-rich ordered precipitates lowers the alloy's free energy relative to the homogeneous disordered BCC state.
Slow cooling provides sufficient Al mobility for local chemical ordering.
Local Al ordering during slow cooling triggers transformation of the homogeneous BCC alloy into a two-phase microstructure containing ordered precipitates.
Rapid quenching suppresses Al redistribution and ordering.
Suppressing Al redistribution by rapid quenching retains a metastable, largely single-phase BCC structure.
Cooling at approximately 1°C/min from above 1000°C will promote Al diffusion and ordering relative to water quenching.
The structural mediator is the diffusion-induced formation of Al-rich, chemically ordered precipitates within a BCC matrix.
The ordered precipitates are likely to have an L1_2-type or similar ordered structure.
The free-energy advantage of the precipitate-containing state over disordered BCC increases as the alloy cools.
Slow-cooled samples will contain distributed Al-rich ordered precipitates in a BCC matrix.
Rapidly quenched samples will remain largely single-phase BCC with minimal chemical ordering.
Cooling-rate control of phase stability applies from the high-temperature BCC state down to room temperature when the rate lies in a window that either permits or suppresses diffusion.
Significant compositional inhomogeneity may place the alloy outside the proposed mechanism's applicable regime.
